# AREA 2 — JSON parse error catalog (json-tui v1.4.1, binary `/workspace/executable`)

Everything below was learned purely by running the binary with crafted inputs and
recording stdout/stderr/exit code. The parser behaves exactly like **nlohmann/json
(~3.11.x) `json::parse()` with all defaults** (strict mode, no comments, exceptions
on), with error messages matching that library byte-for-byte, plus an app-level
wrapper that catches `std::exception` and prints it.

## Captures & test material

- Test inputs (raw bytes, one file per case): `/harness/tests/02/cases/<name>.json`
- Runner that generated them: `/harness/tests/02/run_cases.py`
- Per-case captured streams: `/harness/captures/02/cases/<name>.{out,err,code}`
- Digest of all 136 cases (input repr + exit + stdout repr + stderr repr):
  `/harness/captures/02/results.txt`
- PTY capture of one error (shows `\n`→`\r\n` translation): `/harness/captures/02/pty_bad/`

## 1. Error output plumbing (byte-exact)

For ANY parse failure (file argument or stdin):

- **exit code 1**, always.
- **stdout**:
  - file input: completely empty (0 bytes).
  - stdin input: exactly `Reading from stdin...` (20 bytes, NO trailing newline),
    written before parsing. Nothing else.
- **stderr**: exactly
  `0x0A` + `[` + exception-id + `] ` + message + `0x0A`
  i.e. a LEADING `\n`, then the bracketed id, then the message, then ONE trailing `\n`.

Example for file containing `tru` (od dump of stderr):
```
0a 5b 6a 73 6f 6e 2e 65 78 63 65 70 74 69 6f 6e  >.[json.exception<
2e 70 61 72 73 65 5f 65 72 72 6f 72 2e 31 30 31  >.parse_error.101<
5d 20 70 61 72 73 65 20 65 72 72 6f 72 20 61 74  >] parse error at<
20 6c 69 6e 65 20 31 2c 20 63 6f 6c 75 6d 6e 20  > line 1, column <
34 3a ...                                    >4: ...<
```
full text: `\n[json.exception.parse_error.101] parse error at line 1, column 4: syntax error while parsing value - invalid literal; last read: 'tru'\n`

- **PTY caveat (matters for byte-exact PTY reproduction!)**: on the error path the
  app never touches termios (the TUI is never started), so the PTY's default ONLCR
  output processing rewrites every `\n` on stderr/stdout to `\r\n`. Verified with
  pty2.py: `...last read: 'tru'\r\n` and leading `\r\n`. When stdout is a pipe/file
  there is no translation. So in a PTY the error block appears as
  `\r\n[json.exception.parse_error.101] ...'tru'\r\n`.
- No "Reading from stdin..." is printed for file input. Error text is identical for
  file vs stdin input.

## 2. Position counting rules (line/column)

The `line L, column C` in the message follows nlohmann's lexer position semantics:

- **Line 1-based, column 1-based.** First byte of input is line 1, column 1 (`x` →
  `line 1, column 1`).
- **Column counts BYTES consumed on the current line, not characters.** The reported
  column = number of `get()` calls on the current line INCLUDING the offending byte
  (or the EOF/NUL read). Examples:
  - `tru` (EOF after 3 bytes) → column 4 (the failing read counts).
  - `x` → column 1.
  - `  x` → column 3.
  - `["\xc3\xa9", x]` (é = 2 bytes) → error at `x`, **column 8** (byte index), i.e.
    column counts bytes. `["\xc3\xa9\xc3\xa9" x]` → column 9.
- **Tab advances the column by exactly 1** (no tab stops): `[\t1,\t]` errors on `]`
  at column 6.
- **Only `\n` (0x0A) increments the line number** and resets the column. `\r` (0x0D)
  is just another byte:
  - `[1,\r\n2,]` → error at line 2, column 3 (`\r` consumed a column on line 1).
  - `[1,\r2,]` → line 1, column 7.
- Newline consumed *inside* a string error: the `\n` bumps the line and resets the
  column to 0, so `"a\nb` reports **line 2, column 0** (column 0 is possible!).
- A UTF-8 BOM at the start (see §8) IS counted: input = only BOM → error at
  `line 1, column 4` (3 BOM bytes + failing EOF read).
- A NUL byte (0x00) outside strings acts as end-of-input (see §7) and still counts
  as one consumed column: ` \x00` → column 2; `[1,\x002]` → column 4.

## 3. Message grammar

All parse errors are id `json.exception.parse_error.101` with message:

```
parse error at line L, column C: syntax error while parsing CONTEXT - DETAIL[; last read: 'TOKEN'][; expected EXPECTATION]
```

CONTEXT is one of (verified): `value`, `object key`, `object separator`, `object`,
`array`. Note lowercase `value` — the baseline note saying `VALUE` was WRONG.

EXCEPTION: two messages have no "syntax error while parsing" part:
- empty-ish input: `parse error at line 1, column 1: attempting to parse an empty input; check that your input string or stream contains the expected JSON`
- number overflow uses a different exception id entirely (§5).

### 3.1 Empty / whitespace-only input

| input bytes | message |
|---|---|
| `` (0 bytes) | `line 1, column 1: attempting to parse an empty input; check that your input string or stream contains the expected JSON` |
| `\x00` (single NUL) | identical to empty input (NUL = EOF, §7) |
| ` ` | `line 1, column 2: syntax error while parsing value - unexpected end of input; expected '[', '{', or a literal` |
| `\n` | same but `line 2, column 1` |
| ` \t\r\n  ` | same but `line 2, column 3` |

So: truly-empty (first read is EOF/NUL) → "attempting to parse an empty input";
whitespace then EOF → "unexpected end of input; expected '[', '{', or a literal".

### 3.2 Invalid literals / unexpected characters

DETAIL = `invalid literal; last read: 'TOKEN'`. The literal scanner is
keyword-directed: first byte selects `true`/`false`/`null` expectation; mismatch or
EOF stops immediately. Case-sensitive; `NaN`, `Infinity`, `nan`, `inf`, `True`,
`NULL`, `undefined`, `+1` are all just "invalid literal". Examples:

| input | line, column | last read |
|---|---|---|
| `tru` | 1, 4 | `'tru'` |
| `trux` | 1, 4 | `'trux'` |
| `nul` | 1, 4 | `'nul'` |
| `nuL` | 1, 3 | `'nuL'` (mismatch at 3rd byte) |
| `fals` | 1, 5 | `'fals'` |
| `n` | 1, 2 | `'n'` |
| `x` | 1, 1 | `'x'` |
| `NaN` | 1, 1 | `'N'` |
| `nan` | 1, 2 | `'na'` (tries `null`: n ok, u≠a fails) |
| `Infinity` | 1, 1 | `'I'` |
| `+1` | 1, 1 | `'+'` |
| `.5` | 1, 1 | `'.'` |
| `'abc'` | 1, 1 | `'''` (single quotes NOT supported; `'` in last-read is unescaped) |
| `\x0b1` / `\x0c1` | 1, 1 | `'<U+000B>'` / `'<U+000C>'` (VT/FF are NOT JSON whitespace) |
| `\xff` | 1, 1 | `'\xff'` (raw byte, NOT `<U+...>`) |
| `\xef\xbb\xbf` alone (BOM then EOF) | 1, 4 | (no last-read part; "unexpected end of input...") |

When the invalid literal appears AFTER a complete top-level value, the message gains
`; expected end of input` and the last-read token spans back to the previous token
boundary:
- `truex` → col 5, `invalid literal; last read: 'truex'; expected end of input`
- `[] x` → col 4, `last read: '[] x'; expected end of input`
- `[1] y` → col 5, `last read: '1] y'; expected end of input`
- `0x10` → col 2, `last read: '0x'; expected end of input`
- `1.2.3` → col 4, `last read: '1.2.'; expected end of input`
- `[1] // comment` → col 5, `last read: '1] /'; expected end of input`
- `[1]\n\nx` → line 3 col 1, `last read: '1]<U+000A><U+000A>x'; expected end of input`
- `1\xef...` (BOM after value) → col 2, `last read: '1\xef'; expected end of input`

Inside structures the same "invalid literal" DETAIL occurs with `expected ']'` etc.:
- `["éé" x]` → `while parsing array - invalid literal; last read: '"\xc3\xa9\xc3\xa9" x'; expected ']'`
- `{a:1}` → `while parsing object key - invalid literal; last read: '{a'; expected string literal`

### 3.3 Token-vs-expectation errors (no "last read")

When the next TOKEN is well-formed but wrong for the position, DETAIL is
`unexpected TOKEN; expected EXPECTATION` with NO `last read` part. TOKEN names
observed: `']'`, `'}'`, `','`, `':'`, `'{'`, `number literal`, `string literal`,
`true literal`, `false literal`, `null literal`, `end of input`.

| input | message (after column) |
|---|---|
| `]` | `value - unexpected ']'; expected '[', '{', or a literal` |
| `}` | `value - unexpected '}'; expected '[', '{', or a literal` |
| `[` | `value - unexpected end of input; expected '[', '{', or a literal` |
| `[1` | `array - unexpected end of input; expected ']'` |
| `[1,` | `value - unexpected end of input; expected '[', '{', or a literal` |
| `[1,2` | `array - unexpected end of input; expected ']'` |
| `{` | `object key - unexpected end of input; expected string literal` |
| `{"a"` | `object separator - unexpected end of input; expected ':'` |
| `{"a":` | `value - unexpected end of input; expected '[', '{', or a literal` |
| `{"a":1` | `object - unexpected end of input; expected '}'` |
| `{"a":1,` | `object key - unexpected end of input; expected string literal` |
| `[]]` | `value - unexpected ']'; expected end of input` |
| `{}}` | `value - unexpected '}'; expected end of input` |
| `[1 2]` | `array - unexpected number literal; expected ']'` (col 4) |
| `{"a" 1}` | `object separator - unexpected number literal; expected ':'` (col 6) |
| `{"a":1 "b":2}` | `object - unexpected string literal; expected '}'` (col 10) |
| `{"a",1}` | `object separator - unexpected ','; expected ':'` (col 5) |
| `[1,]` | `value - unexpected ']'; expected '[', '{', or a literal` (col 4) |
| `{"a":1,}` | `object key - unexpected '}'; expected string literal` (col 8) |
| `[,1]` | `value - unexpected ','; expected '[', '{', or a literal` (col 2) |
| `{,}` | `object key - unexpected ','; expected string literal` (col 2) |
| `[1,,2]` | `value - unexpected ','; ...` (col 4) |
| `[1:2]` | `array - unexpected ':'; expected ']'` (col 3) |
| `1 2` | `value - unexpected number literal; expected end of input` (col 3) |
| `true false` | `value - unexpected false literal; expected end of input` (col 10) |
| `truefalse` | `value - unexpected false literal; expected end of input` (col 9) |
| `{} {}` | `value - unexpected '{'; expected end of input` (col 4) |
| `1,` | `value - unexpected ','; expected end of input` (col 2) |
| `null null` | `value - unexpected null literal; expected end of input` (col 9) |
| `"a" "b"` | `value - unexpected string literal; expected end of input` (col 7) |
| `01`, `00` | `value - unexpected number literal; expected end of input` (col 2). NOTE: `0` parses as a complete number, then `1` is an extra token. There is NO "leading zero" specific error. |

Comments are NOT supported: `/* c */ 1` → invalid literal `'/'` at col 1;
`[1, /* x */ 2]` → invalid literal `'1, /'` at col 5.

### 3.4 String errors

All have CONTEXT `value` (or `object key` for keys) and DETAIL starting
`invalid string: ...` plus `last read`. Catalog:

- Unterminated: `invalid string: missing closing quote; last read: '"abc'`
  (`"abc` → col 5; `"` → col 2). As object key: `{"` →
  `object key - invalid string: missing closing quote; last read: '"'; expected string literal` (col 3).
- Bad escape: `invalid string: forbidden character after backslash; last read: '"a\x'`
  — `"\q"` col 3, `"a\ b"` col 4, `"abc\` (escape at EOF) col 6.
  Only `\" \\ \/ \b \f \n \r \t \u` are valid escapes.
- Short/bad `\u`: `invalid string: '\u' must be followed by 4 hex digits; last read: '"\u12"'`
  — `"\u12"` col 6 (note last-read INCLUDES the closing quote here), `"\u12` col 6,
  `"\u12g4"` col 6 with last read `'"\u12g'`. Uppercase/mixed hex ARE accepted
  (`"\uABCD"`, `"\u00e9"` parse fine).
- Lone high surrogate: `invalid string: surrogate U+D800..U+DBFF must be followed by U+DC00..U+DFFF`
  — `"\uD800"` col 8 last read `'"\uD800"'`; `"\uD800x"` col 8 last read `'"\uD800x'`;
  `"\uD800A"` col 13 last read `'"\uD800A'` (the full second escape is
  consumed/validated first); `"\uD800\uD800"` col 13; `"\uD800\` (EOF) col 9;
  `"\uD800\u12"` → the hex-digits error takes precedence (col 12).
- Lone low surrogate: `invalid string: surrogate U+DC00..U+DFFF must follow U+D800..U+DBFF`
  — `"\uDC00"` col 7, last read `'"\uDC00'` (error raised after 4th hex digit, before
  the closing quote is read; contrast with the high-surrogate case which reads one
  more char).
- Valid pair `"\uD800\uDC00"` parses; the string contains U+10000 (UTF-8 `f0 90 80 80`).
- Raw control characters (0x00–0x1F) inside strings:
  `invalid string: control character U+XXXX (NAME) must be escaped to \uXXXX[ or \E]; last read: '"a<U+XXXX>'`
  - NAME is the classic ASCII abbreviation — ALL 32 verified:
    00 NUL, 01 SOH, 02 STX, 03 ETX, 04 EOT, 05 ENQ, 06 ACK, 07 BEL, 08 BS, 09 HT,
    0A LF, 0B VT, 0C FF, 0D CR, 0E SO, 0F SI, 10 DLE, 11 DC1, 12 DC2, 13 DC3,
    14 DC4, 15 NAK, 16 SYN, 17 ETB, 18 CAN, 19 EM, 1A SUB, 1B ESC, 1C FS, 1D GS,
    1E RS, 1F US.
  - Hex in the message is UPPERCASE 4-digit: `U+0009`, `\u0009`.
  - The ` or \E` suffix appears ONLY for 08 (`\b`), 09 (`\t`), 0A (`\n`), 0C (`\f`),
    0D (`\r`). e.g. tab: `control character U+0009 (HT) must be escaped to \u0009 or \t`;
    NUL: `...escaped to \u0000` (no suffix).
  - Position: error at the control byte itself, e.g. `"a\tb"` → col 3. A raw `\n` in
    a string reports `line 2, column 0` (see §2).
  - `0x7F` (DEL) is NOT treated as a control character — `"\x7f"` parses fine.

### 3.5 "last read" token rendering rules

- The token buffer is NOT reset between tokens — it accumulates everything read
  since the beginning that hasn't been consumed by a *completed* value... in
  practice it spans back across previous structural tokens: `[1] // comment` →
  `'1] /'`; `[] x` → `'[] x'`; deep nesting `[[[[...x` (10000 `[`) → the last-read
  contains ALL 10000 `[` plus `x` (stderr was 10138 bytes; NO truncation ever
  observed).
- Rendering of special bytes inside `last read: '...'`:
  - bytes 0x00–0x1F → `<U+XXXX>` (uppercase hex), e.g. newline → `<U+000A>`,
    NUL → `<U+0000>` (`tru\x00e` → `'tru<U+0000>'`).
  - all other bytes are emitted RAW, including `'`, `"`, `\`, DEL (0x7F), invalid
    UTF-8 bytes (0x80–0xFF). E.g. `'abc'` input → `last read: '''`;
    `\xff` → `last read: '\xff'` (raw 0xff byte in stderr);
    `[] \x7f` → `last read: '[] \x7f'`.
- UTF-8 multi-byte sequences that are invalid: the raw bytes read so far are shown.

## 4. Numbers

### 4.1 Lexical errors

| input | col | DETAIL |
|---|---|---|
| `-` | 2 | `invalid number; expected digit after '-'; last read: '-'` |
| `-x` | 2 | same; last read `'-x'` |
| `-.5` | 2 | same; last read `'-.'` |
| `1.` | 3 | `invalid number; expected digit after '.'; last read: '1.'` |
| `1e` | 3 | `invalid number; expected '+', '-', or digit after exponent; last read: '1e'` |
| `1e+`, `1e-` | 4 | `invalid number; expected digit after exponent sign; last read: '1e+'` |
| `.5` | 1 | `invalid literal; last read: '.'` (not a number error) |
| `+1` | 1 | `invalid literal; last read: '+'` |
| `0x10` | 2 | `invalid literal; last read: '0x'; expected end of input` |
| `01`, `00` | 2 | `unexpected number literal; expected end of input` |

`1e01`, `1E2`, `0e0`, `-0`, `-0.0` are all VALID (exponent may have leading zeros).

### 4.2 Value ranges (parsed OK vs error)

The parser produces int64 / uint64 / double exactly like nlohmann:

- Integer without `.`/`e`: negative → int64 if ≥ -2^63; non-negative → int64 if
  ≤ 2^63-1, else uint64 if ≤ 2^64-1, else **silently falls back to double**.
  - `9223372036854775807` → int, displays `9223372036854775807`
  - `9223372036854775808` → uint64, displays `9223372036854775808`
  - `18446744073709551615` (2^64-1) → uint64, displays exact
  - `18446744073709551616` (2^64) → double, displays `1.8446744073709552e+19`
  - `-9223372036854775808` → int64 min, displays exact
  - `-9223372036854775809` → double, displays `-9.223372036854776e+18`
  - 39-digit integer → double `1.2345678901234568e+38` (no error!)
- Any literal with `.` or `e` → double. If the rounded value overflows double
  (|v| > ~1.7976931348623157e308), the app catches
  `json.exception.out_of_range.406`:
  stderr = `\n[json.exception.out_of_range.406] number overflow parsing 'TOKEN'\n`,
  exit 1. TOKEN is the exact source text of the number (e.g. `'1.5e999'`,
  `'-1.5e999'`, `'1e999'`, `'2e308'`, `'1.8e308'`). NO line/column info. Same
  message inside structures (`[1e999]`, `{"a":1e999}`).
  - `1.7e308` parses (displays `1.7e+308`); `1.8e308` errors.
- Underflow is silent: `1.5e-999` → `0.0`; `1e-324` → `0.0`; `4e-324` and
  `2.5e-324` round to the min subnormal, display `5e-324`; `5e-324` → `5e-324`.
- Display of doubles (for the rendering area, recorded here since observed):
  integral doubles get `.0` appended (`1e2` → `100.0`, `1e01` → `10.0`,
  `0e0` → `0.0`); `-0.0` → `-0.0`; `0.5e+10` → `5000000000.0`; `0.1` → `0.1`;
  shortest-round-trip style otherwise.

## 5. UTF-8 validation

Input must be well-formed UTF-8. Violations inside strings:
`invalid string: ill-formed UTF-8 byte; last read: '...'` — examples:
- `"\xff"` → col 2, last read `'"\xff'` (raw byte in message)
- `"\xc0\xaf"` (overlong) → col 2, last read `'"\xc0'`
- `"\x80"` (lone continuation) → col 2
- `"\xf5\x80\x80\x80"` (> U+10FFFF lead) → col 2, last read `'"\xf5'`
- `"\xf4\x90\x80\x80"` (U+110000) → col 3, last read `'"\xf4\x90'`
- `"\xed\xa0\x80"` (UTF-8-encoded surrogate) → col 3, last read `'"\xed\xa0'`
- `"\xe2\x82"` (truncated sequence then quote) → col 4, last read `'"\xe2\x82"'`
- in a key: `{"\xc3":1}` → CONTEXT `object key`, col 4,
  `last read: '"\xc3"'; expected string literal`

Invalid bytes OUTSIDE strings are NOT UTF-8-checked — they hit the literal scanner:
`\xff` alone → `invalid literal; last read: '\xff'` at col 1;
`[] \xc3\xa9` → `invalid literal; last read: '[] \xc3'` (only the first byte
consumed) `; expected end of input`.

Accepted: 2-byte minimum `\xc2\x80`, 4-byte max `\xf4\x8f\xbf\xbf` (U+10FFFF),
normal multi-byte keys/values.

## 6. NUL byte (0x00) semantics — IMPORTANT quirk

Outside strings, a 0x00 byte is treated as **end of input**, and everything after
it is IGNORED:
- `1\x00garbage` → parses as `1`, exit 0, TUI shows `1`.
- `[1]\x00[2]` → parses as `[1]`, exit 0.
- `\x00` alone → identical to empty input ("attempting to parse an empty input").
- `[1,\x002]` → `unexpected end of input; expected '[', '{', or a literal` at col 4.
- Exception: inside a literal scan the NUL is consumed and shown as `<U+0000>`:
  `tru\x00e` → `invalid literal; last read: 'tru<U+0000>'` col 4.
- Inside strings, raw 0x00 is a normal control-character error (§3.4); escaped
  `` is a valid string char.

## 7. BOM handling

- UTF-8 BOM `EF BB BF` at the very start: silently skipped, but its 3 bytes count
  toward the column. `\xef\xbb\xbf{}` parses (shows `{}`); BOM alone →
  `unexpected end of input` at col 4. A BOM anywhere else is just 3 bytes of
  garbage (`1\xef\xbb\xbf` → invalid literal `'1\xef'` col 2).
- UTF-16 LE/BE BOMs are NOT recognized: `\xff\xfe...` → invalid literal `'\xff'`
  col 1; `\xfe\xff...` → `'\xfe'` col 1. Raw UTF-16 without BOM also fails
  (`{\x00}\x00` → `object key - unexpected end of input` col 2, because the NUL
  after `{` acts as EOF).

## 8. Duplicate keys & key order (parse-time semantics)

- Duplicate keys: **LAST value wins**, silently. `{"a":1,"a":2}` displays `"a": 2`.
  `{"a":1,"b":9,"a":2}` displays a:2, b:9.
- Object keys are stored SORTED (std::map byte-lexicographic order), NOT insertion
  order: `{"b":1,"a":2}` displays a then b;
  `{"B":1,"a":2,"A":3,"10":4,"2":5}` displays in order `"10","2","A","B","a"`.

## 9. Nesting depth limit (STACK OVERFLOW — segfault, not an error message!)

There is NO parser-imposed depth limit; deep nesting crashes the process with
SIGSEGV (shell: exit 139; subprocess returncode -11), producing NO stdout/stderr
output at all on file input (on stdin input, `Reading from stdin...` has already
been printed). Measured on this machine (default `ulimit -s` = 8192 KiB):

- nested empty arrays `[[[...]]]` : depth **10470 OK**, depth **10471 SIGSEGV**.
- nested arrays with scalar bottom `[[...1...]]`: 10464 OK / 10465 crash.
- nested objects `{"a":{"a":...1...}}`: depth **11895 OK**, depth **11896 SIGSEGV**.

So the limit is stack-size-dependent (reimplementation should expect the threshold
to move with `ulimit -s`; treat it as "recursive post-parse processing overflows
the default 8 MiB stack at ~10.5k array depth"). Notably, a parse ERROR at great
depth does NOT crash: `[[[...(30000 '[')...x` cleanly prints
`... column 30001: ... invalid literal; last read: '[[[[...x'` — the crash happens
only for successfully-parsed deep documents (post-parse traversal), not in the
recursive-descent parse itself.

## 10. Valid edge cases that MUST parse (display notes)

All of these parse and launch the TUI (exit 0 after `q`); the scalar is rendered
on a single inverted row with its color:
- `true`/`false` → bright yellow (`\x1b[93m`), `null` → bright red (`\x1b[91m`),
  numbers bright cyan (`96`), strings bright green (`92`), keys bright blue (`94`).
- Top-level scalars are fine: `true`, `null`, `0`, `"hello"`.
- `NaN`, `Infinity`, `nan`, `inf`, `undefined` are REJECTED (invalid literal).
- Trailing whitespace (space/tab/CR/LF) after the value is fine: `1\n`, `[1] \t\r\n`.
- `\x7f` (DEL) inside a string parses, but the DEL byte is dropped from the
  DISPLAYED string (`"a\x7fb"` renders `"ab"`); same for an escaped ``
  (`"a\u0000b"` renders `"ab"`) and `\t` inside a string renders as nothing.
  (Rendering details belong to the display area; noted here only as "parses OK".)
- A string containing an escaped newline `"a\nb"` renders across TWO rows, both
  fully inverted — parse-wise it's fine.

## 11. Summary of accepted grammar

Strict RFC 8259 JSON as implemented by nlohmann/json defaults:
- whitespace = exactly space, `\t`, `\n`, `\r` (VT/FF rejected).
- literals: `true` `false` `null` only, lowercase only.
- strings: double quotes only (single quotes rejected); escapes
  `\" \\ \/ \b \f \n \r \t \uXXXX`; surrogate pairs validated; raw control chars
  < 0x20 rejected; DEL allowed; strict UTF-8 validation.
- numbers: JSON grammar (`-?(0|[1-9]\d*)(\.\d+)?([eE][+-]?\d+)?`); no `+`, no
  leading `.`, no trailing `.`, no hex; leading-zero integers actually tokenize as
  `0` + extra token → "unexpected number literal; expected end of input".
- no comments, no trailing commas, no unquoted keys, single top-level value,
  trailing whitespace allowed, trailing garbage rejected with
  `expected end of input`.

## 12. Determinism

Everything above is fully deterministic — same input bytes always give the same
output bytes and exit code; no timing, locale, or environment dependence was
observed on the error paths (TERM etc. irrelevant since the TUI never starts).
The only environment-sensitive item is the §9 segfault threshold (depends on stack
size `ulimit -s`). All error-path output goes through the app's catch-all, so the
leading `\n` + trailing `\n` framing is uniform for both `parse_error.101` and
`out_of_range.406`.

# AREA 2 — JSON parse error catalog (json-tui v1.4.1, binary `/workspace/executable`)

Everything below was learned purely by running the binary with crafted inputs and
recording stdout/stderr/exit code. The parser behaves exactly like **nlohmann/json
(~3.11.x) `json::parse()` with all defaults** (strict mode, no comments, exceptions
on), with error messages matching that library byte-for-byte, plus an app-level
wrapper that catches `std::exception` and prints it.

## Captures & test material

- Test inputs (raw bytes, one file per case): `/harness/tests/02/cases/<name>.json`
- Runner that generated them: `/harness/tests/02/run_cases.py`
- Per-case captured streams: `/harness/captures/02/cases/<name>.{out,err,code}`
- Digest of all 136 cases (input repr + exit + stdout repr + stderr repr):
  `/harness/captures/02/results.txt`
- PTY capture of one error (shows `\n`→`\r\n` translation): `/harness/captures/02/pty_bad/`

## 1. Error output plumbing (byte-exact)

For ANY parse failure (file argument or stdin):

- **exit code 1**, always.
- **stdout**:
  - file input: completely empty (0 bytes).
  - stdin input: exactly `Reading from stdin...` (20 bytes, NO trailing newline),
    written before parsing. Nothing else.
- **stderr**: exactly
  `0x0A` + `[` + exception-id + `] ` + message + `0x0A`
  i.e. a LEADING `\n`, then the bracketed id, then the message, then ONE trailing `\n`.

Example for file containing `tru` (od dump of stderr):
```
0a 5b 6a 73 6f 6e 2e 65 78 63 65 70 74 69 6f 6e  >.[json.exception<
2e 70 61 72 73 65 5f 65 72 72 6f 72 2e 31 30 31  >.parse_error.101<
5d 20 70 61 72 73 65 20 65 72 72 6f 72 20 61 74  >] parse error at<
20 6c 69 6e 65 20 31 2c 20 63 6f 6c 75 6d 6e 20  > line 1, column <
34 3a ...                                    >4: ...<
```
full text: `\n[json.exception.parse_error.101] parse error at line 1, column 4: syntax error while parsing value - invalid literal; last read: 'tru'\n`

- **PTY caveat (matters for byte-exact PTY reproduction!)**: on the error path the
  app never touches termios (the TUI is never started), so the PTY's default ONLCR
  output processing rewrites every `\n` on stderr/stdout to `\r\n`. Verified with
  pty2.py: `...last read: 'tru'\r\n` and leading `\r\n`. When stdout is a pipe/file
  there is no translation. So in a PTY the error block appears as
  `\r\n[json.exception.parse_error.101] ...'tru'\r\n`.
- No "Reading from stdin..." is printed for file input. Error text is identical for
  file vs stdin input.

## 2. Position counting rules (line/column)

The `line L, column C` in the message follows nlohmann's lexer position semantics:

- **Line 1-based, column 1-based.** First byte of input is line 1, column 1 (`x` →
  `line 1, column 1`).
- **Column counts BYTES consumed on the current line, not characters.** The reported
  column = number of `get()` calls on the current line INCLUDING the offending byte
  (or the EOF/NUL read). Examples:
  - `tru` (EOF after 3 bytes) → column 4 (the failing read counts).
  - `x` → column 1.
  - `  x` → column 3.
  - `["\xc3\xa9", x]` (é = 2 bytes) → error at `x`, **column 8** (byte index), i.e.
    column counts bytes. `["\xc3\xa9\xc3\xa9" x]` → column 9.
- **Tab advances the column by exactly 1** (no tab stops): `[\t1,\t]` errors on `]`
  at column 6.
- **Only `\n` (0x0A) increments the line number** and resets the column. `\r` (0x0D)
  is just another byte:
  - `[1,\r\n2,]` → error at line 2, column 3 (`\r` consumed a column on line 1).
  - `[1,\r2,]` → line 1, column 7.
- Newline consumed *inside* a string error: the `\n` bumps the line and resets the
  column to 0, so `"a\nb` reports **line 2, column 0** (column 0 is possible!).
- A UTF-8 BOM at the start (see §8) IS counted: input = only BOM → error at
  `line 1, column 4` (3 BOM bytes + failing EOF read).
- A NUL byte (0x00) outside strings acts as end-of-input (see §7) and still counts
  as one consumed column: ` \x00` → column 2; `[1,\x002]` → column 4.

## 3. Message grammar

All parse errors are id `json.exception.parse_error.101` with message:

```
parse error at line L, column C: syntax error while parsing CONTEXT - DETAIL[; last read: 'TOKEN'][; expected EXPECTATION]
```

CONTEXT is one of (verified): `value`, `object key`, `object separator`, `object`,
`array`. Note lowercase `value` — the baseline note saying `VALUE` was WRONG.

EXCEPTION: two messages have no "syntax error while parsing" part:
- empty-ish input: `parse error at line 1, column 1: attempting to parse an empty input; check that your input string or stream contains the expected JSON`
- number overflow uses a different exception id entirely (§5).

### 3.1 Empty / whitespace-only input

| input bytes | message |
|---|---|
| `` (0 bytes) | `line 1, column 1: attempting to parse an empty input; check that your input string or stream contains the expected JSON` |
| `\x00` (single NUL) | identical to empty input (NUL = EOF, §7) |
| ` ` | `line 1, column 2: syntax error while parsing value - unexpected end of input; expected '[', '{', or a literal` |
| `\n` | same but `line 2, column 1` |
| ` \t\r\n  ` | same but `line 2, column 3` |

So: truly-empty (first read is EOF/NUL) → "attempting to parse an empty input";
whitespace then EOF → "unexpected end of input; expected '[', '{', or a literal".

### 3.2 Invalid literals / unexpected characters

DETAIL = `invalid literal; last read: 'TOKEN'`. The literal scanner is
keyword-directed: first byte selects `true`/`false`/`null` expectation; mismatch or
EOF stops immediately. Case-sensitive; `NaN`, `Infinity`, `nan`, `inf`, `True`,
`NULL`, `undefined`, `+1` are all just "invalid literal". Examples:

| input | line, column | last read |
|---|---|---|
| `tru` | 1, 4 | `'tru'` |
| `trux` | 1, 4 | `'trux'` |
| `nul` | 1, 4 | `'nul'` |
| `nuL` | 1, 3 | `'nuL'` (mismatch at 3rd byte) |
| `fals` | 1, 5 | `'fals'` |
| `n` | 1, 2 | `'n'` |
| `x` | 1, 1 | `'x'` |
| `NaN` | 1, 1 | `'N'` |
| `nan` | 1, 2 | `'na'` (tries `null`: n ok, u≠a fails) |
| `Infinity` | 1, 1 | `'I'` |
| `+1` | 1, 1 | `'+'` |
| `.5` | 1, 1 | `'.'` |
| `'abc'` | 1, 1 | `'''` (single quotes NOT supported; `'` in last-read is unescaped) |
| `\x0b1` / `\x0c1` | 1, 1 | `'<U+000B>'` / `'<U+000C>'` (VT/FF are NOT JSON whitespace) |
| `\xff` | 1, 1 | `'\xff'` (raw byte, NOT `<U+...>`) |
| `\xef\xbb\xbf` alone (BOM then EOF) | 1, 4 | (no last-read part; "unexpected end of input...") |

When the invalid literal appears AFTER a complete top-level value, the message gains
`; expected end of input` and the last-read token spans back to the previous token
boundary:
- `truex` → col 5, `invalid literal; last read: 'truex'; expected end of input`
- `[] x` → col 4, `last read: '[] x'; expected end of input`
- `[1] y` → col 5, `last read: '1] y'; expected end of input`
- `0x10` → col 2, `last read: '0x'; expected end of input`
- `1.2.3` → col 4, `last read: '1.2.'; expected end of input`
- `[1] // comment` → col 5, `last read: '1] /'; expected end of input`
- `[1]\n\nx` → line 3 col 1, `last read: '1]<U+000A><U+000A>x'; expected end of input`
- `1\xef...` (BOM after value) → col 2, `last read: '1\xef'; expected end of input`

Inside structures the same "invalid literal" DETAIL occurs with `expected ']'` etc.:
- `["éé" x]` → `while parsing array - invalid literal; last read: '"\xc3\xa9\xc3\xa9" x'; expected ']'`
- `{a:1}` → `while parsing object key - invalid literal; last read: '{a'; expected string literal`

### 3.3 Token-vs-expectation errors (no "last read")

When the next TOKEN is well-formed but wrong for the position, DETAIL is
`unexpected TOKEN; expected EXPECTATION` with NO `last read` part. TOKEN names
observed: `']'`, `'}'`, `','`, `':'`, `'{'`, `number literal`, `string literal`,
`true literal`, `false literal`, `null literal`, `end of input`.

| input | message (after column) |
|---|---|
| `]` | `value - unexpected ']'; expected '[', '{', or a literal` |
| `}` | `value - unexpected '}'; expected '[', '{', or a literal` |
| `[` | `value - unexpected end of input; expected '[', '{', or a literal` |
| `[1` | `array - unexpected end of input; expected ']'` |
| `[1,` | `value - unexpected end of input; expected '[', '{', or a literal` |
| `[1,2` | `array - unexpected end of input; expected ']'` |
| `{` | `object key - unexpected end of input; expected string literal` |
| `{"a"` | `object separator - unexpected end of input; expected ':'` |
| `{"a":` | `value - unexpected end of input; expected '[', '{', or a literal` |
| `{"a":1` | `object - unexpected end of input; expected '}'` |
| `{"a":1,` | `object key - unexpected end of input; expected string literal` |
| `[]]` | `value - unexpected ']'; expected end of input` |
| `{}}` | `value - unexpected '}'; expected end of input` |
| `[1 2]` | `array - unexpected number literal; expected ']'` (col 4) |
| `{"a" 1}` | `object separator - unexpected number literal; expected ':'` (col 6) |
| `{"a":1 "b":2}` | `object - unexpected string literal; expected '}'` (col 10) |
| `{"a",1}` | `object separator - unexpected ','; expected ':'` (col 5) |
| `[1,]` | `value - unexpected ']'; expected '[', '{', or a literal` (col 4) |
| `{"a":1,}` | `object key - unexpected '}'; expected string literal` (col 8) |
| `[,1]` | `value - unexpected ','; expected '[', '{', or a literal` (col 2) |
| `{,}` | `object key - unexpected ','; expected string literal` (col 2) |
| `[1,,2]` | `value - unexpected ','; ...` (col 4) |
| `[1:2]` | `array - unexpected ':'; expected ']'` (col 3) |
| `1 2` | `value - unexpected number literal; expected end of input` (col 3) |
| `true false` | `value - unexpected false literal; expected end of input` (col 10) |
| `truefalse` | `value - unexpected false literal; expected end of input` (col 9) |
| `{} {}` | `value - unexpected '{'; expected end of input` (col 4) |
| `1,` | `value - unexpected ','; expected end of input` (col 2) |
| `null null` | `value - unexpected null literal; expected end of input` (col 9) |
| `"a" "b"` | `value - unexpected string literal; expected end of input` (col 7) |
| `01`, `00` | `value - unexpected number literal; expected end of input` (col 2). NOTE: `0` parses as a complete number, then `1` is an extra token. There is NO "leading zero" specific error. |

Comments are NOT supported: `/* c */ 1` → invalid literal `'/'` at col 1;
`[1, /* x */ 2]` → invalid literal `'1, /'` at col 5.

### 3.4 String errors

All have CONTEXT `value` (or `object key` for keys) and DETAIL starting
`invalid string: ...` plus `last read`. Catalog:

- Unterminated: `invalid string: missing closing quote; last read: '"abc'`
  (`"abc` → col 5; `"` → col 2). As object key: `{"` →
  `object key - invalid string: missing closing quote; last read: '"'; expected string literal` (col 3).
- Bad escape: `invalid string: forbidden character after backslash; last read: '"a\x'`
  — `"\q"` col 3, `"a\ b"` col 4, `"abc\` (escape at EOF) col 6.
  Only `\" \\ \/ \b \f \n \r \t \u` are valid escapes.
- Short/bad `\u`: `invalid string: '\u' must be followed by 4 hex digits; last read: '"\u12"'`
  — `"\u12"` col 6 (note last-read INCLUDES the closing quote here), `"\u12` col 6,
  `"\u12g4"` col 6 with last read `'"\u12g'`. Uppercase/mixed hex ARE accepted
  (`"\uABCD"`, `"\u00e9"` parse fine).
- Lone high surrogate: `invalid string: surrogate U+D800..U+DBFF must be followed by U+DC00..U+DFFF`
  — `"\uD800"` col 8 last read `'"\uD800"'`; `"\uD800x"` col 8 last read `'"\uD800x'`;
  `"\uD800A"` col 13 last read `'"\uD800A'` (the full second escape is
  consumed/validated first); `"\uD800\uD800"` col 13; `"\uD800\` (EOF) col 9;
  `"\uD800\u12"` → the hex-digits error takes precedence (col 12).
- Lone low surrogate: `invalid string: surrogate U+DC00..U+DFFF must follow U+D800..U+DBFF`
  — `"\uDC00"` col 7, last read `'"\uDC00'` (error raised after 4th hex digit, before
  the closing quote is read; contrast with the high-surrogate case which reads one
  more char).
- Valid pair `"\uD800\uDC00"` parses; the string contains U+10000 (UTF-8 `f0 90 80 80`).
- Raw control characters (0x00–0x1F) inside strings:
  `invalid string: control character U+XXXX (NAME) must be escaped to \uXXXX[ or \E]; last read: '"a<U+XXXX>'`
  - NAME is the classic ASCII abbreviation — ALL 32 verified:
    00 NUL, 01 SOH, 02 STX, 03 ETX, 04 EOT, 05 ENQ, 06 ACK, 07 BEL, 08 BS, 09 HT,
    0A LF, 0B VT, 0C FF, 0D CR, 0E SO, 0F SI, 10 DLE, 11 DC1, 12 DC2, 13 DC3,
    14 DC4, 15 NAK, 16 SYN, 17 ETB, 18 CAN, 19 EM, 1A SUB, 1B ESC, 1C FS, 1D GS,
    1E RS, 1F US.
  - Hex in the message is UPPERCASE 4-digit: `U+0009`, `\u0009`.
  - The ` or \E` suffix appears ONLY for 08 (`\b`), 09 (`\t`), 0A (`\n`), 0C (`\f`),
    0D (`\r`). e.g. tab: `control character U+0009 (HT) must be escaped to \u0009 or \t`;
    NUL: `...escaped to \u0000` (no suffix).
  - Position: error at the control byte itself, e.g. `"a\tb"` → col 3. A raw `\n` in
    a string reports `line 2, column 0` (see §2).
  - `0x7F` (DEL) is NOT treated as a control character — `"\x7f"` parses fine.

### 3.5 "last read" token rendering rules

- The token buffer is NOT reset between tokens — it accumulates everything read
  since the beginning that hasn't been consumed by a *completed* value... in
  practice it spans back across previous structural tokens: `[1] // comment` →
  `'1] /'`; `[] x` → `'[] x'`; deep nesting `[[[[...x` (10000 `[`) → the last-read
  contains ALL 10000 `[` plus `x` (stderr was 10138 bytes; NO truncation ever
  observed).
- Rendering of special bytes inside `last read: '...'`:
  - bytes 0x00–0x1F → `<U+XXXX>` (uppercase hex), e.g. newline → `<U+000A>`,
    NUL → `<U+0000>` (`tru\x00e` → `'tru<U+0000>'`).
  - all other bytes are emitted RAW, including `'`, `"`, `\`, DEL (0x7F), invalid
    UTF-8 bytes (0x80–0xFF). E.g. `'abc'` input → `last read: '''`;
    `\xff` → `last read: '\xff'` (raw 0xff byte in stderr);
    `[] \x7f` → `last read: '[] \x7f'`.
- UTF-8 multi-byte sequences that are invalid: the raw bytes read so far are shown.

## 4. Numbers

### 4.1 Lexical errors

| input | col | DETAIL |
|---|---|---|
| `-` | 2 | `invalid number; expected digit after '-'; last read: '-'` |
| `-x` | 2 | same; last read `'-x'` |
| `-.5` | 2 | same; last read `'-.'` |
| `1.` | 3 | `invalid number; expected digit after '.'; last read: '1.'` |
| `1e` | 3 | `invalid number; expected '+', '-', or digit after exponent; last read: '1e'` |
| `1e+`, `1e-` | 4 | `invalid number; expected digit after exponent sign; last read: '1e+'` |
| `.5` | 1 | `invalid literal; last read: '.'` (not a number error) |
| `+1` | 1 | `invalid literal; last read: '+'` |
| `0x10` | 2 | `invalid literal; last read: '0x'; expected end of input` |
| `01`, `00` | 2 | `unexpected number literal; expected end of input` |

`1e01`, `1E2`, `0e0`, `-0`, `-0.0` are all VALID (exponent may have leading zeros).

### 4.2 Value ranges (parsed OK vs error)

The parser produces int64 / uint64 / double exactly like nlohmann:

- Integer without `.`/`e`: negative → int64 if ≥ -2^63; non-negative → int64 if
  ≤ 2^63-1, else uint64 if ≤ 2^64-1, else **silently falls back to double**.
  - `9223372036854775807` → int, displays `9223372036854775807`
  - `9223372036854775808` → uint64, displays `9223372036854775808`
  - `18446744073709551615` (2^64-1) → uint64, displays exact
  - `18446744073709551616` (2^64) → double, displays `1.8446744073709552e+19`
  - `-9223372036854775808` → int64 min, displays exact
  - `-9223372036854775809` → double, displays `-9.223372036854776e+18`
  - 39-digit integer → double `1.2345678901234568e+38` (no error!)
- Any literal with `.` or `e` → double. If the rounded value overflows double
  (|v| > ~1.7976931348623157e308), the app catches
  `json.exception.out_of_range.406`:
  stderr = `\n[json.exception.out_of_range.406] number overflow parsing 'TOKEN'\n`,
  exit 1. TOKEN is the exact source text of the number (e.g. `'1.5e999'`,
  `'-1.5e999'`, `'1e999'`, `'2e308'`, `'1.8e308'`). NO line/column info. Same
  message inside structures (`[1e999]`, `{"a":1e999}`).
  - `1.7e308` parses (displays `1.7e+308`); `1.8e308` errors.
- Underflow is silent: `1.5e-999` → `0.0`; `1e-324` → `0.0`; `4e-324` and
  `2.5e-324` round to the min subnormal, display `5e-324`; `5e-324` → `5e-324`.
- Display of doubles (for the rendering area, recorded here since observed):
  integral doubles get `.0` appended (`1e2` → `100.0`, `1e01` → `10.0`,
  `0e0` → `0.0`); `-0.0` → `-0.0`; `0.5e+10` → `5000000000.0`; `0.1` → `0.1`;
  shortest-round-trip style otherwise.

## 5. UTF-8 validation

Input must be well-formed UTF-8. Violations inside strings:
`invalid string: ill-formed UTF-8 byte; last read: '...'` — examples:
- `"\xff"` → col 2, last read `'"\xff'` (raw byte in message)
- `"\xc0\xaf"` (overlong) → col 2, last read `'"\xc0'`
- `"\x80"` (lone continuation) → col 2
- `"\xf5\x80\x80\x80"` (> U+10FFFF lead) → col 2, last read `'"\xf5'`
- `"\xf4\x90\x80\x80"` (U+110000) → col 3, last read `'"\xf4\x90'`
- `"\xed\xa0\x80"` (UTF-8-encoded surrogate) → col 3, last read `'"\xed\xa0'`
- `"\xe2\x82"` (truncated sequence then quote) → col 4, last read `'"\xe2\x82"'`
- in a key: `{"\xc3":1}` → CONTEXT `object key`, col 4,
  `last read: '"\xc3"'; expected string literal`

Invalid bytes OUTSIDE strings are NOT UTF-8-checked — they hit the literal scanner:
`\xff` alone → `invalid literal; last read: '\xff'` at col 1;
`[] \xc3\xa9` → `invalid literal; last read: '[] \xc3'` (only the first byte
consumed) `; expected end of input`.

Accepted: 2-byte minimum `\xc2\x80`, 4-byte max `\xf4\x8f\xbf\xbf` (U+10FFFF),
normal multi-byte keys/values.

## 6. NUL byte (0x00) semantics — IMPORTANT quirk

Outside strings, a 0x00 byte is treated as **end of input**, and everything after
it is IGNORED:
- `1\x00garbage` → parses as `1`, exit 0, TUI shows `1`.
- `[1]\x00[2]` → parses as `[1]`, exit 0.
- `\x00` alone → identical to empty input ("attempting to parse an empty input").
- `[1,\x002]` → `unexpected end of input; expected '[', '{', or a literal` at col 4.
- Exception: inside a literal scan the NUL is consumed and shown as `<U+0000>`:
  `tru\x00e` → `invalid literal; last read: 'tru<U+0000>'` col 4.
- Inside strings, raw 0x00 is a normal control-character error (§3.4); escaped
  `` is a valid string char.

## 7. BOM handling

- UTF-8 BOM `EF BB BF` at the very start: silently skipped, but its 3 bytes count
  toward the column. `\xef\xbb\xbf{}` parses (shows `{}`); BOM alone →
  `unexpected end of input` at col 4. A BOM anywhere else is just 3 bytes of
  garbage (`1\xef\xbb\xbf` → invalid literal `'1\xef'` col 2).
- UTF-16 LE/BE BOMs are NOT recognized: `\xff\xfe...` → invalid literal `'\xff'`
  col 1; `\xfe\xff...` → `'\xfe'` col 1. Raw UTF-16 without BOM also fails
  (`{\x00}\x00` → `object key - unexpected end of input` col 2, because the NUL
  after `{` acts as EOF).

## 8. Duplicate keys & key order (parse-time semantics)

- Duplicate keys: **LAST value wins**, silently. `{"a":1,"a":2}` displays `"a": 2`.
  `{"a":1,"b":9,"a":2}` displays a:2, b:9.
- Object keys are stored SORTED (std::map byte-lexicographic order), NOT insertion
  order: `{"b":1,"a":2}` displays a then b;
  `{"B":1,"a":2,"A":3,"10":4,"2":5}` displays in order `"10","2","A","B","a"`.

## 9. Nesting depth limit (STACK OVERFLOW — segfault, not an error message!)

There is NO parser-imposed depth limit; deep nesting crashes the process with
SIGSEGV (shell: exit 139; subprocess returncode -11), producing NO stdout/stderr
output at all on file input (on stdin input, `Reading from stdin...` has already
been printed). Measured on this machine (default `ulimit -s` = 8192 KiB):

- nested empty arrays `[[[...]]]` : depth **10470 OK**, depth **10471 SIGSEGV**.
- nested arrays with scalar bottom `[[...1...]]`: 10464 OK / 10465 crash.
- nested objects `{"a":{"a":...1...}}`: depth **11895 OK**, depth **11896 SIGSEGV**.

So the limit is stack-size-dependent (reimplementation should expect the threshold
to move with `ulimit -s`; treat it as "recursive post-parse processing overflows
the default 8 MiB stack at ~10.5k array depth"). Notably, a parse ERROR at great
depth does NOT crash: `[[[...(30000 '[')...x` cleanly prints
`... column 30001: ... invalid literal; last read: '[[[[...x'` — the crash happens
only for successfully-parsed deep documents (post-parse traversal), not in the
recursive-descent parse itself.

## 10. Valid edge cases that MUST parse (display notes)

All of these parse and launch the TUI (exit 0 after `q`); the scalar is rendered
on a single inverted row with its color:
- `true`/`false` → bright yellow (`\x1b[93m`), `null` → bright red (`\x1b[91m`),
  numbers bright cyan (`96`), strings bright green (`92`), keys bright blue (`94`).
- Top-level scalars are fine: `true`, `null`, `0`, `"hello"`.
- `NaN`, `Infinity`, `nan`, `inf`, `undefined` are REJECTED (invalid literal).
- Trailing whitespace (space/tab/CR/LF) after the value is fine: `1\n`, `[1] \t\r\n`.
- `\x7f` (DEL) inside a string parses, but the DEL byte is dropped from the
  DISPLAYED string (`"a\x7fb"` renders `"ab"`); same for an escaped ``
  (`"a\u0000b"` renders `"ab"`) and `\t` inside a string renders as nothing.
  (Rendering details belong to the display area; noted here only as "parses OK".)
- A string containing an escaped newline `"a\nb"` renders across TWO rows, both
  fully inverted — parse-wise it's fine.

## 11. Summary of accepted grammar

Strict RFC 8259 JSON as implemented by nlohmann/json defaults:
- whitespace = exactly space, `\t`, `\n`, `\r` (VT/FF rejected).
- literals: `true` `false` `null` only, lowercase only.
- strings: double quotes only (single quotes rejected); escapes
  `\" \\ \/ \b \f \n \r \t \uXXXX`; surrogate pairs validated; raw control chars
  < 0x20 rejected; DEL allowed; strict UTF-8 validation.
- numbers: JSON grammar (`-?(0|[1-9]\d*)(\.\d+)?([eE][+-]?\d+)?`); no `+`, no
  leading `.`, no trailing `.`, no hex; leading-zero integers actually tokenize as
  `0` + extra token → "unexpected number literal; expected end of input".
- no comments, no trailing commas, no unquoted keys, single top-level value,
  trailing whitespace allowed, trailing garbage rejected with
  `expected end of input`.

## 12. Determinism

Everything above is fully deterministic — same input bytes always give the same
output bytes and exit code; no timing, locale, or environment dependence was
observed on the error paths (TERM etc. irrelevant since the TUI never starts).
The only environment-sensitive item is the §9 segfault threshold (depends on stack
size `ulimit -s`). All error-path output goes through the app's catch-all, so the
leading `\n` + trailing `\n` framing is uniform for both `parse_error.101` and
`out_of_range.406`.

payload.resultSummary:
Area 2 is complete. Deliverable written to `/harness/notes/02-parse-errors.md` (407 lines).

## What I did

Built a batch runner (`/harness/tests/02/run_cases.py`) that executes `/workspace/executable` on 136 crafted malformed/edge inputs (raw bytes stored in `/harness/tests/02/cases/*.json`), capturing stdout/stderr/exit code per case (`/harness/captures/02/cases/*.{out,err,code}`, digest in `/harness/captures/02/results.txt`). Followed up with targeted probes for stdin path, float-overflow boundaries, key ordering, NUL-byte semantics, all 32 control-char names, UTF-8 validation edges, and a binary search for the nesting-depth limit. Verified one error case through `pty2.py` (capture in `/harness/captures/02/pty_bad/`) to confirm PTY behavior.

## Key findings (all in the notes, byte-exact)

- **Error plumbing**: exit 1 always; stderr = `\n[json.exception.<id>] <message>\n`; stdout empty for file input, exactly `Reading from stdin...` (no newline) for stdin. In a PTY the error path never touches termios, so ONLCR turns every `\n` into `\r\n`.
- Parser is behaviorally identical to nlohmann/json ~3.11 strict `parse()`; the baseline note's `VALUE` is wrong — context names are lowercase (`value`, `object key`, `object separator`, `object`, `array`).
- **Position rules**: line 1-based on `\n` only (`\r` is just a column byte); column counts **bytes** (UTF-8 é = 2 columns, tab = 1), includes the failing read; newline inside a string error can yield `column 0`.
- Full message catalog documented: empty vs whitespace-only input, invalid literals (incl. how `nan`→`'na'`, case-sensitivity, `+1`, `.5`), every string error variant (unterminated, bad escape, `\u` hex, lone high/low surrogates, all 32 control-char messages with the ` or \b/\t/\n/\f/\r` suffix rule), token-vs-expectation errors (trailing commas, missing colons, `01` tokenizing as `0`+extra), `last read` rendering (raw bytes for ≥0x7F, `<U+XXXX>` for <0x20, no truncation — a 10000-`[` token is dumped in full).
- **Numbers**: int64→uint64→double fallback is silent for big integers (2^64 → `1.8446744073709552e+19`); double overflow (>~1.7977e308) throws `out_of_range.406` — `\n[json.exception.out_of_range.406] number overflow parsing 'TOKEN'\n`, no position, even inside structures; underflow silently → `0.0`/`5e-324`.
- **Quirks**: NUL byte outside strings acts as EOF (trailing garbage after `\x00` is ignored!); UTF-8 BOM skipped but counts 3 columns; UTF-16 BOMs rejected; duplicate keys → last wins; keys stored sorted byte-lexicographically (`"10","2","A","B","a"`).
- **Depth limit**: no parser limit — deep nesting SIGSEGVs (no output, exit 139) at **10471** nested arrays / **11896** nested objects with the default 8 MiB stack (`ulimit -s 8192`); a parse *error* at depth 30000 still reports cleanly, so the crash is in post-parse processing. Flagged as stack-size-dependent, hence environment-sensitive.
- Valid-edge confirmations: `NaN`/`Infinity`/single quotes/comments/trailing commas all rejected; DEL (0x7F) allowed in strings; `\uABCD` uppercase hex fine; trailing whitespace fine.

Nothing left undone for this area. The only non-deterministic item is the segfault threshold (stack-size dependent); everything else was byte-stable across runs.

args.content:
# Area 06 — Table view

Raw captures: `/harness/captures/06/` (each subdir has `step0.bin` = initial frame,
`stepN.bin` = output after Nth input token). Test JSON inputs: `/harness/tests/06/`
and inline in this file. All captures made with `/harness/pty2.py` on 80x24 unless
noted otherwise.

## 1. Trigger conditions (which arrays get a table view)

An array gets a table view **iff it has >= 2 elements AND every element is a JSON
object** (empty objects `{}` count). Verified:

| input | marker? |
|---|---|
| `[{"a":1,"b":"x"},{"a":2,"b":"y"},{"a":3,"b":"z"}]` | YES |
| `[{"a":1}]` (single element) | NO |
| `[]` | NO |
| `[{}]` (single empty object) | NO |
| `[{},{}]` / `[{}, {}, {}]` | YES (degenerate table, §7) |
| `[{"a":1},{"b":2}]` (disjoint keys) | YES |
| `[{"a":1},{}]` | YES |
| `[1,2,3]` | NO |
| `[[1,2],[3,4]]` | NO |
| `[{"a":1},2]` (mixed) | NO |
| `[{"a":1},{"a":2},null]` | NO |

The marker appears wherever the array appears: expanded root `[   (table view)`,
collapsed `[...]   (table view)`, and nested, e.g. `"x": [...]   (table view)`.
Exact form in array view (initial, row selected): the `[` is inverted, then
3 spaces, then the grey marker:

```
\x1b[7m[\x1b[27m   \x1b[90m\x1b[49m(table view)\x1b[39m\x1b[49m
```

i.e. marker text is `(table view)` in `\x1b[90m\x1b[49m ... \x1b[39m\x1b[49m`
(bright-black/grey), always separated from `[` / `[...]` by exactly 3 spaces.

## 2. Entering / leaving table view

The marker is a focusable button. Three ways to toggle:

- **TAB** in array view: moves focus from the JSON row to the button. The marker
  becomes inverted: `\x1b[7m\x1b[90m\x1b[49m(table view)\x1b[27m\x1b[39m\x1b[49m`,
  the `[` loses its inversion, cursor moves to the `)` (last char of the button
  text, e.g. x=15 when the line is `[   (table view)`).
  Pressing TAB again moves focus back to the JSON row (it toggles node<->button;
  with several tables in one document TAB still only toggles the button of the
  currently selected node — verified with
  `{"t1": [{"a":1},{"a":2}], "t2": [{"b":3},{"b":4}]}`).
- **ENTER** (or **SPACE**, untested but SPACE==ENTER elsewhere) on the focused
  button: switches to table view. The whole array row is replaced by the button
  line `(array view)` (same grey/inverse styling) followed by the table.
- **Mouse click** on the button toggles directly (verified: SGR mouse
  `\x1b[<0;6;1M` + release on the marker switched to table view in one step).

In table view, ENTER on the focused `(array view)` button switches back to array
view; the array is restored in its previous (expanded) state, focus on the button.

When table view opens, focus is on the button (inverse row 0, cursor on the `)`
of `(array view)`, x=11 since the button is at column 0).

## 3. Table layout — exact structure

Example `[{"a":1,"b":"x"},{"a":2,"b":"y"},{"a":3,"b":"z"}]` in table view
(capture `03_tabenter/step2.bin`):

```
(array view)
 ┏━┳━━━┓
 ┃a┃b  ┃
 ┡━╇━━━┩
0│1│"x"│
1│2│"y"│
2│3│"z"│
 └─┴───┘
```

Line structure:

1. **Button line**: `(array view)` — grey (`90m/49m ... 39m/49m`); wrapped in
   `\x1b[7m...\x1b[27m` when focused. No leading space.
2. **Top border**: ` ` + `┏` + (`━`*w_i + `┳`) per column, last `┓` — i.e.
   leading plain space, then heavy top border over the key columns only.
3. **Header line**: leading space in grey (`\x1b[90m\x1b[49m \x1b[39m\x1b[49m`,
   this is the empty index-column header cell), then per column:
   `┃` + key text + space-padding, all with NO SGR (default color), header text
   left-aligned, padded to column width with plain spaces. Ends with `┃`.
4. **Header separator**: ` ` + `┡` + (`━`*w_i + `╇`) per column + `┩`.
5. **Body rows** (one or more terminal lines each, see §5): index digits in grey
   (`90m/49m ... 39m/49m`), left-aligned in the index column, NO surrounding
   border on the left; then per column `│` + cell. Cell = value with its type
   color, padded with spaces to column width; the padding is INSIDE the color
   region: `\x1b[96m\x1b[49m1 \x1b[39m\x1b[49m`. Separators `│` are plain.
   Continuation lines of a multi-line row have a grey space in the index column.
6. **Bottom border**: ` ` + `└` + (`─`*w_i + `┴`) per column + `┘`.

Box-drawing characters (UTF-8):
- Top: `┏` U+250F, `━` U+2501, `┳` U+2533, `┓` U+2513 (all HEAVY)
- Header verticals: `┃` U+2503 (heavy)
- Header separator: `┡` U+2521, `╇` U+2547, `┩` U+2529, horizontals `━` U+2501 (heavy)
- Body verticals: `│` U+2502 (light)
- Bottom: `└` U+2514, `─` U+2500, `┴` U+2534, `┘` U+2518 (all LIGHT)

Note the mix: top/header heavy, body/bottom light. There are NO horizontal
separators between body rows.

**Index column**: width = number of decimal digits of the largest index
(rows 0..9 → width 1, 10+ rows → width 2, etc.). Left-aligned, digits grey.
It sits OUTSIDE the table's left border; its "header" is a grey space, and on
border lines its position is a plain leading space.

**Frame width / padding**: every line of the frame is padded with plain spaces
to the frame width = width of the widest line (usually the table; if the table
is narrower than the 12-char button line, the table lines are padded to 12 —
see `03_tabenter/step2.bin` where every border/body line has 4 trailing spaces).
Lines are joined with `\r\r\n`; the last line is not followed by `\r\r\n`.
Frame followed by cursor-reposition + `\x1b[?25l` + `\x00` as usual.

## 4. Columns: order, content, widths

- **Column set** = union of all keys of all objects. **Order = sorted
  lexicographically** (byte-wise; verified `b,a,c,d` input → `a b c d`;
  `arr name nested` for `{"name","nested","arr"}`). NOT first-object order.
- **Missing key** in a row → empty cell: plain spaces, no SGR at all.
- **Cell values** use the same colors as the main view:
  number `\x1b[96m`, string `\x1b[92m` (rendered WITH quotes, e.g. `"x"`),
  boolean (true AND false) `\x1b[93m`, null `\x1b[91m`,
  each closed by `\x1b[39m\x1b[49m`. Number formatting as in main view
  (`1.50` → `1.5`, `-2e3` → `-2000.0`).
- **Natural column width** = max(header text width, max over rows of cell
  content width). Widths are display-cell widths (wcwidth): `"héllo wörld"` → 13
  (é/ö width 1), `"中文字"` → 8 (CJK width 2). Header-only example:
  `longname` column with 1-digit cells → width 8.
- **Index column** never shrinks and is not counted in the shrink algorithm.

## 5. Nested values inside cells

- Array value → always the collapsed literal `[...]` in bold
  (`\x1b[1m[...]\x1b[22m`), even for `[]`. One line.
- Object value → rendered EXPANDED as a mini JSON tree inside the cell, one key
  per line, 2-space indent, with all ITS container children collapsed:
  ```
  {
    "p": {...},
    "r": [...]
  }
  ```
  The opening `{` of the cell and the `{...},` / `[...]` literals are bold;
  keys `94m`; the closing `}` is plain. Trailing commas inside the cell as in
  the main view. The row becomes as many terminal lines tall as the tallest
  cell; shorter cells in the same row pad with blank (space) lines; continuation
  lines start with grey-space index cell + `│`.
- These nested `{...}` / `[...]` inside cells are focusable and ENTER-expandable
  in place (see §6).

## 6. Selection / navigation inside table view

Focus model: the button and every non-empty cell (and every expandable line
inside multi-line cells) are focusable; the SELECTED element's first line is
drawn inverted.

- **DOWN from button** → first cell (column 0) of body row 0.
- **UP/DOWN** move between rows keeping the column; UP from row 0 → button.
  DOWN from the last row: stays. The header/separator/border lines and the
  index column are never focusable.
- **LEFT/RIGHT** move between cells of the current row; at the edges: stays.
- **Only the cell's value is inverted**, not the whole row and not the padding.
  Exact bytes for a selected number cell (from `06_nav/step3.bin`):
  `\x1b[7m\x1b[96m\x1b[49m1\x1b[27m\x1b[39m\x1b[49m` — note the pad space that
  is normally inside the color region is dropped for the selected cell (only
  the bare value text is wrapped). Separators and index stay non-inverted.
- **Cursor position** = last display column of the focused element's first
  line: on a cell, x = cell_start + column_width - 1; on the button, the `)`.
- **Empty (missing-key) cells are not focusable**: RIGHT onto an empty cell is
  blocked (selection stays). DOWN onto a row where the current column is empty
  lands on the FIRST non-empty cell of that row (verified: from (row0,"b")
  DOWN → (row1,"a") when row1.b is missing). A row whose object is `{}` (all
  cells empty) is not focusable at all — DOWN is blocked.
- **TAB** on a body cell cycles through the cells of the CURRENT ROW ONLY
  (wraps within the row); it does not reach other rows or the button.
- **ENTER** on a focused collapsed container inside a cell (`{...}`) expands it
  in place (cell grows, table re-layouts); ENTER on the expanded content
  collapses it back. ENTER on primitive cells: nothing.
- **`+` / `-`** in table view: no visible effect (tested on button and on
  expanded cell content).
- **`g` `g` (two separate keystrokes)** jumps to the LAST body row; **`G`**
  jumps to the button (top). NOTE: this is the opposite of the README's
  gg=top/G=bottom and looks inverted relative to the main view too — flag for
  the navigation area. TIMING ANOMALY: sending `gg` as one write (one pty2
  token) did NOT move the selection in table view, while two separate `g`
  tokens (0.25 s apart) did. In the main array view the single-token `gg` DID
  jump (to the bottom). Treat `gg` behavior as timing-sensitive and
  cross-check with area 05.
- Tall tables scroll with the normal vertical scrolling (whole frame including
  the button scrolls off; see `24_tall/`, 20x8 terminal, 12-row table).

## 7. Degenerate table: array of empty objects

`[{},{}]` (capture `14_emptyobj/step2.bin`) — zero key columns. The index
column moves INSIDE the borders and becomes the only column:

```
(array view)
┏━┓
┃ ┃
┡━┩
│0│
│1│
└─┘
```

- No leading space on border lines.
- Header line: `┃` + grey space + `┃`.
- Body: `│` + grey index + `│`.
- Column width 1 (index digits).

## 8. Width-shrink algorithm (table wider than terminal)

Natural table line width = index_w + Σ(col_i + 1) + 1 (index column, one
border per column, right border). If this exceeds the terminal width, the key
columns shrink (index column and borders never do; button line does NOT shrink
— it is hard-truncated at the terminal width, e.g. `(array vie` at cols=10).

Let `w_i` = natural widths, `W = Σ w_i`, `A = term_cols - (index_w + ncols + 1)`
(available total for cells), `B = W - A` (shrink budget, when > 0):

- base shrink per column: `s_i = floor(w_i * B / W)`
- remainder `R = B - Σ s_i` (always < ncols): distribute 1 extra unit per
  column starting from the LAST column and moving left.

Verified data points:

| natural widths | term cols | result |
|---|---|---|
| 6,6,6 | 17 (A=12,B=6) | 4,4,4 |
| 6,6,6 | 16 (B=7) | 4,4,3 |
| 6,6,6 | 15 (B=8) | 4,3,3 |
| 6,6,6 | 14 (B=9) | 3,3,3 |
| 5,2,2 | 12 (A=7,B=2) | 4,2,1 |
| 5,2,2 | 10 (A=5,B=4) | 3,1,1 |
| 62,2 | 30 (A=26,B=38) | 26,0 |

Columns can shrink to width 0 (header text and cell content disappear; only
the two bordering `┃`/`│` remain). Cell content wider than the shrunk column is
hard-TRUNCATED (no ellipsis, cut mid-string, e.g. `"a very long string that `).
Strings never wrap in cells. If the table fits, it keeps its natural width
(does NOT expand to fill the terminal).

Truncation cuts whole display cells; multi-line (object) cells under shrink:
not explicitly probed — recommend the implementer test object cells in a
narrow terminal.

## 9. Cursor/quit misc

- `-` with focus on the table button: nothing. ESC / q quit as usual.
- In table view the `(array view)` button line is NOT inverted when a cell is
  focused: plain `\x1b[90m\x1b[49m(array view)\x1b[39m\x1b[49m`.
- Cursor reposition after a table frame: e.g. small 3-row table ends with
  `\x1b[7A\x1b[1D\x1b[?25l\x00` (from bottom-right corner back to the focused

- `01_arrobj/` — initial array view with marker (full od in notes §1).
- `03_tabenter/` — TAB focus + ENTER into table (od'd fully, §3).
- `04_missing/` — disjoint keys, union/sorted columns, empty cells (od'd, §4).
- `05_nested/` — object expanded vs array `[...]` in cells (§5).
- `06_nav/`, `07_back/`, `08_cells/` — cell navigation, toggle back (§6).
- `09_tabcycle/` — TAB wraps within current row.
- `10_longcell/`, `11_narrow/` — long string, 30-col shrink.
- `12_many/` — 12 rows, 2-digit index (§3).
- `13_deep/` — nested containers in cells (od'd, §5).
- `14_emptyobj/` — `[{},{}]` degenerate table (od'd, §7).
- `15_deepnav/` — ENTER-expand inside cells.
- `16_minus/` — `-` does nothing in table view.
- `17_gg/`, `18_G/`, `19_g/` — gg/G behavior + timing anomaly (§6).
- `20_emptycells/`, `21_downempty/` — empty-cell focus rules.
- `22_click/` — mouse click on button toggles.
- `23_unicode/` — é and CJK width measurement.
- `24_tall/` — 20x8 terminal, scrolling.
- `25_togglecell/`, `26_emptyrow/`, `27_two/` — cell ENTER toggle, empty row
  blocked, TAB with two tables.
- `/tmp`-based probes (not kept): single-element array, mixed arrays, width
  table in §8 (re-run recipes inline in this file).

Nothing else non-deterministic was observed beyond the `gg` timing anomaly in §6.

(available total for cells), `B = W - A` (shrink budget, when > 0):

- base shrink per column: `s_i = floor(w_i * B / W)`
- remainder `R = B - Σ s_i` (always < ncols): distribute 1 extra unit per
  column starting from the LAST column and moving left.

| natural widths | term cols | result |
|---|---|---|
| 6,6,6 | 17 (A=12,B=6) | 4,4,4 |
| 6,6,6 | 16 (B=7) | 4,4,3 |
| 6,6,6 | 15 (B=8) | 4,3,3 |
| 6,6,6 | 14 (B=9) | 3,3,3 |
| 5,2,2 | 12 (A=7,B=2) | 4,2,1 |
| 5,2,2 | 10 (A=5,B=4) | 3,1,1 |
| 62,2 | 30 (A=26,B=38) | 26,0 |

Columns can shrink to width 0 (header text and cell content disappear; only
the two bordering `┃`/`│` remain). Cell content wider than the shrunk column is
hard-TRUNCATED (no ellipsis, cut mid-string, e.g. `"a very long string that `).
Strings never wrap in cells. If the table fits, it keeps its natural width
(does NOT expand to fill the terminal).

Truncation cuts whole display cells; multi-line (object) cells under shrink:
not explicitly probed — recommend the implementer test object cells in a
narrow terminal.

payload.resultSummary:
Area 6 (Table view) is fully documented. Deliverable written to `/harness/notes/06-table.md`; ~20 capture sets in `/harness/captures/06/`; test JSONs in `/harness/tests/06/`.

Key findings (all verified against the binary, byte-level where subtle):

**Trigger**: an array gets the grey `(table view)` marker iff it has **≥2 elements and ALL are objects** (empty `{}` counts; single-element arrays, `[]`, mixed-content arrays do not). Marker appears expanded (`[   (table view)`), collapsed (`[...]   (table view)`), and nested (`"x": [...]   (table view)`), exactly 3 spaces after the bracket, in `90m/49m` grey.

**Toggle**: marker is a button. TAB focuses it (toggles node↔button only, even with multiple tables), ENTER switches views, mouse-click toggles directly. Table view shows `(array view)` button + table; ENTER on it returns to array view with prior state intact.

**Layout** (fully od-dumped): leading-space index column (grey, left-aligned, width = digits of max index) OUTSIDE the left border; heavy top/header (`┏━┳┓┃`, `┡━╇┩` separator), light body/bottom (`│`, `└─┴┘`); no inter-row separators. Columns = **union of all keys, sorted lexicographically** (not first-object order). Column width = max(header, cell widths) in display cells (wcwidth — CJK=2 verified). Missing key → plain-space cell, no SGR. Cell colors match main view (96m num, 92m quoted string, 93m bool, 91m null; bold `{`/`[...]`). Frame lines space-padded to widest line, joined `\r\r\n`.

**Nested cells**: arrays always render `[...]` (one line); objects render EXPANDED as a mini-tree with their children collapsed (`{...}`/`[...]`), making rows multi-line; nested containers are ENTER-expandable in place.

**Width-shrink algorithm** (table wider than terminal), reverse-engineered from 7 data points: `s_i = floor(w_i·B/W)`, remainder distributed 1 per column from the LAST column leftward; columns can shrink to 0; cells hard-truncate (no ellipsis); button line truncates at terminal width; table never expands beyond natural width.

**Selection**: cell-based; only the focused cell is inverted (`\x1b[7m` wraps value+padding inside the color codes). Arrows move cell-to-cell; empty cells aren't focusable (RIGHT blocked; DOWN lands on first non-empty cell of target row; all-empty rows unreachable); TAB cycles within the current row only; `+`/`-` are no-ops; `g`,`g` (separate keystrokes) → last row, `G` → button (inverted vs README). Degenerate `[{},{}]` table puts the index inside the borders as the sole column.

**Flagged non-determinism**: `gg` sent as one write does nothing in table view but works as two separate `g` keystrokes; in main array view one-write `gg` jumps to bottom — timing-sensitive, cross-referenced for area 05. Untested: multi-line (object) cells under narrow-terminal shrink.
